tasks.entryDescription: Goursat triangle subdivision; Green's theorem and Cauchy–Riemann equations; homotopy/primitive arguments on simply connected domains.
tasks.currentSketch: Subdivide a triangle repeatedly into four similar triangles. If integral over original triangle were nonzero, some nested subtriangle has integral at least 4^{-n} times original; shrinking diameter and complex differentiability make its integral o(area), contradiction. Thus triangle integrals vanish; triangulation gives path independence locally.

tasks.currentSketch: For holomorphic f=u+iv, Cauchy–Riemann makes the relevant curl zero. Green's theorem then gives ∮f dz=0 for a region bounded by a suitable curve; excision/triangulation extends the result under regularity assumptions.

tasks.routeTitle: homotopy/primitive arguments on simply connected domains
tasks.currentSketch: On a simply connected domain, integrals around null-homotopic loops vanish by homotopy invariance (which itself follows from local Cauchy theorem). Then define F(z)=∫_{z0}^z f(w)dw; path independence makes F well-defined and F'=f. This route assumes local theorem, so is not independent globally.

tasks.currentSketch: Cauchy's estimate gives |f'(z0)|≤M/R for entire f bounded by M on every circle centered at z0. Let R→∞; derivative vanishes everywhere, so f is constant.

tasks.entryDescription: Cauchy estimates with radius→∞; mean-value property for harmonic functions; maximum principle on expanding disks.
tasks.currentSketch: The real and imaginary parts of a bounded entire function are bounded harmonic functions. Mean-value property and letting circle radius grow show each value equals its average with vanishing oscillation; hence both are constant.

tasks.entryDescription: Cauchy estimates with radius→∞; mean-value property for harmonic functions; maximum principle on expanding disks.
tasks.currentSketch: A nonconstant holomorphic function is open, so on a large disk its maximum modulus cannot be attained in the interior. If globally bounded, maxima on expanding boundaries and maximum principle force no interior variation; equivalently apply the principle to disks and Cauchy estimates. Needs the maximum-modulus theorem.

tasks.entryDescription: Derive from Goursat's theorem and a small-circle deformation; prove with Green's theorem and the Cauchy–Riemann equations; obtain from the power-series coefficient formula.
tasks.routeTitle: Derive from Goursat's theorem and a small-circle deformation
tasks.currentSketch: For a≠z deform the contour integral of f(ζ)/(ζ−z) from a small circle around z to the outer contour; Cauchy's theorem on the annulus equates them. As radius→0, continuity yields 2πi f(z), giving the formula.

tasks.entryDescription: Derive from Goursat's theorem and a small-circle deformation; prove with Green's theorem and the Cauchy–Riemann equations; obtain from the power-series coefficient formula.
tasks.routeTitle: prove with Green's theorem and the Cauchy–Riemann equations
tasks.currentSketch: Apply Green's theorem to f(ζ)/(ζ−z) on the region with a small disk removed; Cauchy–Riemann makes area term zero, leaving outer boundary equal to inner-circle integral. The latter tends to 2πif(z).

tasks.entryDescription: Derive from Goursat's theorem and a small-circle deformation; prove with Green's theorem and the Cauchy–Riemann equations; obtain from the power-series coefficient formula.
tasks.routeTitle: obtain from the power-series coefficient formula
tasks.currentSketch: Expand f(z+w)=∑a_nw^n on a disk; integrate termwise on a circle. Orthogonality of exponentials isolates a_0=f(z), yielding the integral formula on circles, then contour deformation extends it.

tasks.entryDescription: Sperner's lemma/combinatorial labeling; degree theory; no-retraction theorem and homology.
tasks.currentSketch: Triangulate a simplex finely and label each vertex i by a coordinate where x_i exceeds the corresponding image coordinate under a hypothetical fixed-point-free map. Sperner's lemma gives a fully labeled small simplex; mesh→0 and compactness yield a point with x_i≥f_i(x) all i, hence equality because coordinates sum to one. Balls are homeomorphic to simplex.

tasks.entryDescription: Sperner's lemma/combinatorial labeling; degree theory; no-retraction theorem and homology.
tasks.currentSketch: Define degree of id−f on a ball: if f has no fixed point, id−f avoids zero, so boundary degree is zero; homotopy to identity gives degree one, contradiction. Requires degree theory and boundary condition.

tasks.entryDescription: Sperner's lemma/combinatorial labeling; degree theory; no-retraction theorem and homology.
tasks.currentSketch: A fixed-point-free self-map of a ball would yield a retraction from the ball to its boundary by extending the ray from f(x) through x. But no-retraction follows from homology: inclusion S^{n−1}→B^n induces impossible map on top reduced homology. Thus fixed point exists.

tasks.entryDescription: Local differential-geometric curvature integration; triangulation plus angle defect; index theorem/characteristic classes in generalized forms.
tasks.currentSketch: In an oriented orthonormal frame, moving around a small geodesic triangle changes tangent direction by ∫K dA; boundary turning plus corner exterior angles totals 2π. Subdivide a triangulated surface into such triangles; edge terms cancel and sum angle defects to 2πχ.

tasks.entryDescription: Local differential-geometric curvature integration; triangulation plus angle defect; index theorem/characteristic classes in generalized forms.
tasks.currentSketch: For each triangulated face, angle sum defect is 2π minus its angles; sum over faces and use each interior edge's two angles and vertex angle totals to simplify to 2π(V−E+F). Curvature integral equals summed angular excess in the refinement limit.

tasks.currentSketch: Chern–Weil theory represents Euler class by curvature form; integrating the Euler class over a closed oriented surface gives Euler characteristic. This is a generalized proof via characteristic classes, relying on Chern–Weil and Gauss–Bonnet identification.

tasks.entryDescription: Polygonal approximation and winding number; separation via homology; combinatorial planar graph arguments for polygonal curves. State the curve regularity/version.
tasks.currentSketch: Approximate a Jordan curve by a sufficiently close simple polygon. The polygon has inside/outside; winding number is locally constant off the curve. The annular closeness gives the same index for points away from the curve, and polygonal separation passes to the curve. Careful approximation/compactness is required.

For Galois extension, subextensions correspond to transitive quotient actions/stabilizers, recovering the theorem. This is an advanced reformulation, not an independent proof; requires separability.

tasks.entryDescription: Leading-coefficient ideals and induction; module-theoretic finite generation; Gröbner-basis/monomial ideal argument.
tasks.currentSketch: Let R be Noetherian and I⊂R[x]. Leading coefficients of elements of I form a finitely generated ideal; choose polynomials realizing generators. Above their maximum degree, subtract suitable multiples to reduce degree. The bounded-degree remainder lies in a finite R-module, so its submodule is finite; these elements generate I.

tasks.entryDescription: Leading-coefficient ideals and induction; module-theoretic finite generation; Gröbner-basis/monomial ideal argument.
tasks.currentSketch: Regard R[x] as an R-module filtered by degree. The leading-term coefficient ideal stabilizes finitely; quotient I by the finitely generated leading-term generators has bounded degree and is a submodule of finite free R-module R^{d+1}, hence finitely generated.

tasks.entryDescription: Leading-coefficient ideals and induction; module-theoretic finite generation; Gröbner-basis/monomial ideal argument.
tasks.currentSketch: Choose a monomial order; the ideal of leading monomials is finitely generated by Dickson's lemma. Pick polynomials whose leading monomials generate it; division reduces any f∈I to zero remainder, so these generate I. This proves polynomial-ring Noetherianity when R is Noetherian; coefficients over R need standard Gröbner termination.
